title: Hot-Season Hydraulic Fault Pattern
body: Excavators throwing hydraulic faults in the heat get worked as one-off symptom fixes — a leak here, a slow cylinder there — instead of the fleet-wide root cause they actually are. That's how a machine like EX-263 racks up seven different hydraulic faults in fourteen days: every repair addresses what's in front of the mechanic, never the pump, cooler, or circuit driving all of them.
keyPoints: Heat stress on a hydraulic system doesn't repeat one symptom — it shows up as leaks, slow response, and valve failures on the same machine in the same week. Varied fault descriptions on one unit are a pattern, not five unrelated breakdowns.

A single-day cluster across multiple machines (three excavators plus a borrowed grader all faulting hydraulically on the same day) is a fleet signal, not coincidence — it should trigger a fleet-wide oil-temperature and cooler check, not five separate work orders.

Don't fold every fault into the heat story by default — EX-123's root cause turned out to be a mechanical slew ring failure, not hydraulics. Confirm the mechanism before you file it under "hot season."
Cooler-fin dust blockage compounds heat stress in this environment — cooler condition is part of the check, not just oil temperature.
If a repair only holds for one clean production day before a new symptom appears on the same machine, that's a signal the fix addressed the symptom, not the fault.
apply: Late August is still peak heat — if an excavator throws a hydraulic fault today, check whether it's a fresh isolated issue or another entry in a chain on that same unit before signing off on a symptom-only repair.
